old: A single parameter was admissible at $\pm5\%$ in 15 of the 27 problems examined. In the synthetic prediction experiment the selected subset $S$ predicted better than the best single parameter (smaller $e_{\mathrm{pred}}$) in 9 of the 15 problems where both could be evaluated (Supplementary Table~\ref{tab:single}), but on real data the single parameter had the lower test $\chi^2/n$ in 10 of the 15. These two comparisons are mixed; the test of \sref{kmin} shows that the second parameter acts as a margin of safety: a single parameter is as identifiable and predictive, but fails in more individual scenarios, especially for large changes.
